items.q: Why do heavily mocked unit tests break on every refactor even though behaviour never changed?
items.a:
A test should pin [[g:observable behaviour]], not the path the code walks to produce it. Mock every collaborator and the test becomes a copy of the implementation: change the path and it fails while the system still works. **Two failure modes tell you which mistake you made:** - test red, behaviour unchanged → [[r:test coupled to implementation]] — it verifies calls, not outcomes - behaviour broken, tests green → [[o:the test asserts nothing]] — the mock returned the answer being checked
Implementation testBehaviour test
Assertsa call happenedthe resulting state
Survives refactornoyes
Catches real bugsrarelyusually
Reads likethe codethe requirement
// implementation test — dies the day the service batches its writes
@Test void places_order() {
    service.place(cmd);
    verify(repo).save(any(Order.class));   // a call, not an outcome
}
//
// behaviour test — same requirement, survives the refactor
@Test void placed_order_is_pending_and_holds_stock() {
    var id = service.place(cmd);
    assertThat(orders.find(id).status()).isEqualTo(PENDING);
    assertThat(stock.available(SKU)).isEqualTo(9);
}
:::tip Where verify() still earns its place When the call itself *is* the requirement: an email sent, a payment captured, an event published. Everywhere else, assert on state. ::: :::deep - the [[b:twelve-mock smell]]: if arranging one unit test needs a dozen stubs, the class under test is orchestrating too much. The fix is in the design, not in the test. - mocking a type you do not own (a driver, an SDK client) pins your *assumption* about that library. When the assumption is wrong, the test agrees with you and production does not. - a test that never fails is not protection. Break the production line on purpose and confirm the test goes red — that is the cheap version of mutation testing (26-testing-strategy.testing-what-usually-breaks.q5). - naming carries the requirement: `placed_order_is_pending` survives review; `testPlace1` tells the next reader nothing when it fails at 2am. :::

items.q: Dummy, stub, spy, mock, fake — which double do you reach for, and why do seniors prefer fakes?
items.a:
The five are not synonyms. Picking the wrong one is how a suite becomes brittle.
DoubleWhat it doesUse it when
Dummyfills a parameter, never useda constructor demands an argument you do not exercise
Stubreturns canned answersyou need the collaborator to produce input
Spyrecords what happened, real or partialyou must assert an outbound side effect
Mockpre-programmed with expectationsthe interaction itself is the requirement
Fakea working, simplified implementationthe port has real behaviour: storage, clock, queue
A [[g:fake]] is the one that scales. An in-memory implementation of your repository port gives real semantics — write then read, unique keys collide, ordering holds — with none of the setup: 
class InMemoryOrders implements Orders {
    private final Map<OrderId, Order> db = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    
    public void save(Order o) {
        if (db.putIfAbsent(o.id(), o) != null) throw new DuplicateOrder(o.id());
    }
    public Optional<Order> find(OrderId id) { return Optional.ofNullable(db.get(id)); }
}
Write it once per port and every use-case test gets faster *and* more honest than a pile of `when(...).thenReturn(...)`. :::warn The fake must be tested too A fake that silently accepts duplicates while the real repository rejects them turns green tests into a production incident. Run the same contract test suite against both. ::: :::deep - [[b:classicist vs mockist]]: the classicist tests through real collaborators and mocks only the edges of the system; the mockist mocks every dependency. In backend code the classicist style ages better, because the edges are few and the internals move constantly. - mock only what you [[o:own and control]] — your own ports. For a driver or SDK, prefer an integration test against the real thing in a container (26-testing-strategy.integration-tests-that-tell-the-truth.q1). - [[r:partial mocks]] (`spy()` on the class under test, stubbing one of its own methods) mean the class has two responsibilities. Split it instead. - a fake for the clock is `Clock.fixed(...)`; for the outbox, a list you can assert on; for the payment gateway, a scripted one that can be told to time out — that is the seam every failure test needs. :::

items.q: Which bugs never show up in unit tests, and what does that imply for where you spend test budget?
items.a:
Unit tests cover the code you wrote. Most production incidents come from the places where your code meets something else. **The recurring blind spots:** - SQL and the mapping layer: a wrong join, a lazy association, a missing index, a dialect difference - serialization at the boundary: an unknown field, a date format, a `BigDecimal` losing scale - time and time zones: DST, a fixed `Instant.now()` in the code path, expiry compared across skewed clocks - concurrency: two requests on the same row, a lost update, a race the single-threaded test cannot express - configuration: the value that differs only in production, the profile nobody loads in CI - failure paths: the timeout, the retry, the compensation that has never once been executed
LayerWhat it can proveWhat it cannot
Unitdomain rules, branching, calculationsthat the query is correct or the schema matches
IntegrationSQL, transactions, serialization, migrationsthat two services agree on a contract
Contractproducer and consumer still fitthat the whole flow meets its latency budget
End-to-endthe critical path really worksanything cheaply, or anything about rare branches
That is why the pyramid is a [[o:cost]] argument, not a moral one: put the volume where feedback is fast, and buy a small number of expensive tests exactly where the money is — checkout, payment, auth (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q6). :::tip The question that reallocates budget Take the last five incidents. For each, ask which test would have caught it. The answer is rarely "one more unit test". ::: :::deep - an [[r:untested failure path]] is not a gap in coverage, it is dead code you are relying on. Compensation logic and DLQ handlers are the classic case (09-distributed-tx-fintech.distributed-transaction-patterns.q2). - coverage reports flatter you here: the happy path through a repository is covered, while the constraint violation it must translate never runs. - keep [[g:one end-to-end test per revenue path]] and treat the rest as diagnostics. E2E suites that grow unbounded become the thing everyone reruns until it passes. - if a bug escaped to production, the fix ships with the test that reproduces it — at the cheapest layer that can express it, not always end-to-end. :::

items.q: How do you build test data so the suite stays readable, and where does property-based testing pay off?
items.a:
Shared fixtures are the usual reason a suite becomes unreadable and flaky: every test silently depends on a row someone else inserted, and reordering tests changes results. **Prefer local, explicit, minimal data:** - a builder per aggregate, with sane defaults, overriding only the field the test is about - each test creates what it needs and owns it — no shared "seed" file the whole suite reads - values that carry meaning: `orderWith(total("120.00"), currency("VND"))`, never `new Order(1, 2, "x", true, null)` 
// the builder keeps the requirement visible: this test is about expiry only
var hold = aSeatHold()
        .expiringAt(now.plus(5, MINUTES))
        .build();
//
// property-based: the rule must hold for every split, not for the one you imagined
@Property void split_never_loses_a_cent(@ForAll @IntRange(min=1, max=50) int parts,
                                    @ForAll @BigRange(min="0.01", max="1000000") BigDecimal total) {
    var shares = Money.of(total).splitInto(parts);
    assertThat(shares.stream().reduce(ZERO, BigDecimal::add)).isEqualByComparingTo(total);
}
[[g:Property-based testing]] pays off exactly where examples run out: rounding and money splits, serialization round-trips, parsers, pagination boundaries, idempotency keys, and any invariant of the form *whatever the input, this must still hold*. :::warn Random data without a seed is a flaky test Frameworks report the failing seed — capture it in the failure message and pin it as a regular example test once it finds a bug, otherwise the next run may not reproduce it. ::: :::deep - [[b:round-trip properties]] are the cheapest to write and catch the most: `parse(render(x)) == x` finds date-format, encoding and scale bugs that no hand-written example thought of. - shrinking is the real value — the framework reduces a 40-field failing case to the minimal one, which is usually the bug report itself. - for database tests, prefer [[o:per-test transactional cleanup or a fresh schema]] over a shared seed; ordering dependence is the second most common source of flakiness after time (26-testing-strategy.testing-what-usually-breaks.q5). - an object mother (`Orders.pending()`, `Orders.paid()`) reads better than a builder when the test needs a *state*, not a field. Use both: mother for the state, builder for the one deviation. :::

sections.title: Integration tests that tell the truth

items.q: Why does an H2-backed test suite pass while production fails, and how do you run the real engine without wrecking build time?
items.a:
H2 is a different database wearing a compatibility mode. It agrees with you on `SELECT`, and diverges exactly where the interesting bugs live.
BehaviourH2 in compatibility modeThe real engine
Lockingno gap or next-key locksInnoDB gap locks change what deadlocks (05-db-core-index-lock.transactions-mvcc-locking.q3)
Query plana different optimiser entirelythe plan you tuned for
Typeslooser: dates, numerics, JSONrejects what H2 accepted
DDLmigrations often need an H2 variantthe migration you actually ship
Upsert / window / CTEpartial dialect coveragefull
[[g:Testcontainers]] removes the whole class of problem by starting the engine you deploy. The cost people fear is startup, and it is fixable: 
// one container for the whole JVM, reused by every test class
abstract class DbTest {
    static final PostgreSQLContainer<?> DB =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");
    static { DB.start(); }          // no @Container: do not stop per class
    
    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void props(DynamicPropertyRegistry r) {
        r.add("spring.datasource.url", DB::getJdbcUrl);
        r.add("spring.datasource.username", DB::getUsername);
        r.add("spring.datasource.password", DB::getPassword);
    }
}
**What makes it fast enough in CI:** - one shared container per JVM plus `reuse` locally, instead of one per test class - run the real Flyway/Liquibase migrations once, then clean data between tests, not schema - keep the DB tests in their own task so the unit suite still returns in seconds :::tip What an integration test is for Prove the things only the engine can prove: the SQL, the constraint, the migration, the transaction boundary. Business branching still belongs in fast unit tests. ::: :::deep - migrating with the [[b:same migration tool as production]] is half the value: a broken changelog fails in CI rather than during a deploy window (26-testing-strategy.integration-tests-that-tell-the-truth.q2). - clean between tests by [[o:truncating tables]] or restoring a template database; `@Transactional` rollback is faster but hides flush-time failures. - containers are not only for SQL: Kafka, Redis, LocalStack and a mock OIDC provider all remove a class of "works on my laptop" surprise (03-spring-boot-deep-build.auto-configuration-build.q10). - pin image tags. `postgres:latest` turns an unrelated upstream release into a red build on a Monday morning. - the [[r:one thing H2 still buys you]] is a smoke test that the context loads. That is not worth the false confidence it grants elsewhere. :::

items.q: Why does @Transactional on a test hide real bugs, and how do you test transaction boundaries honestly?
items.a:
A transactional test runs your code inside a transaction that never commits. That is convenient for cleanup and dishonest about everything that happens at commit time. **What the rollback hides:** - constraint violations that only fire on flush or on `COMMIT` (deferred constraints, unique indexes) - the persistence context papering over your query: an entity is returned from the first-level cache, so a broken `SELECT` still passes - `REQUIRES_NEW`, `@TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)` and outbox publishing, none of which behave the same way when the outer transaction is never committed (03-spring-boot-deep-build.ioc-container-transactions.q3) - lock behaviour and deadlocks, since the test holds one long transaction instead of the short ones production runs 
// dishonest: passes even if the entity was never really written
@Test @Transactional void saves_order() {
    orders.save(order);
    assertThat(orders.findById(id)).isPresent();   // served from the 1st-level cache
}
//
// honest: force the write out, then read with fresh eyes
@Test void saves_order() {
    txTemplate.executeWithoutResult(s -> orders.save(order));   // commits
    em.clear();
    assertThat(orders.findById(id)).isPresent();
}
:::warn The rule Use `@Transactional` on tests for read-only setup convenience. The moment the assertion is about persistence, commit for real and clear the persistence context first. ::: :::deep - to test [[g:propagation]] you need two real transactions: call the outer service through the proxy, make the inner one `REQUIRES_NEW`, throw after it, then assert the inner row survived and the outer one did not (03-spring-boot-deep-build.ioc-container-transactions.q2). - [[o:self-invocation]] bugs are invisible to a mock-based test and obvious in an integration test — the annotation on the inner method simply does nothing. - `TestEntityManager#flush` then `clear` is the cheapest way to make an ORM test tell the truth: flush pushes the SQL, clear forces the next read to hit the database. - assert on [[b:what the next request would see]], not on the object you just handed to `save()`. Those two are different things, and every N+1 or stale-read bug lives in the gap. - rollback-based cleanup also hides trigger and `ON CONFLICT` behaviour, which is exactly what idempotency relies on (25-microservice.09-idempotency-the-central-link.q1). :::

items.q: Your Spring test suite takes 14 minutes, mostly starting contexts. What is actually happening and how do you fix it?
items.a:
Spring caches an application context and reuses it across test classes — but the cache key is the [[g:whole configuration]]. Any difference mints a new context and pays the startup cost again. **Everything below is part of that key:** - the set of `@ContextConfiguration` classes and locations - active profiles and `@TestPropertySource` values - `@MockBean` / `@SpyBean` declarations, including which beans they replace - context initializers, `@DirtiesContext` on any test in the class
PatternEffect on the cacheDo instead
A different `@MockBean` combo per classone context per combinationa small number of shared test configurations
`@DirtiesContext` "to be safe"evicts the context, everything after pays againclean the state you dirtied
Per-class propertiesnew key per classone base class per profile
`@SpringBootTest` for pure logicstarts everything for a calculationplain JUnit, no container
// one base per shape of test: two contexts total, not forty
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)
@ActiveProfiles("test")
abstract class AppTest extends DbTest { }
//
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)     // slice: no DB, no Kafka, ~1s
class OrderControllerTest { }
:::tip The measurement that settles the argument Turn on context-loading logs and count how many times the banner prints. If it is more than the number of distinct configurations you intended, that number is your build-time bill. ::: :::deep - slice tests exist to keep the key small: `@WebMvcTest` builds MVC only, `@DataJpaTest` the persistence layer only. They start in about a second and cover serialization, validation and mapping — the parts most likely to break at the boundary. - [[r:@MockBean is not free]]: besides forking the context, it re-introduces the implementation coupling that unit tests were supposed to avoid. Prefer a test configuration that supplies a fake bean. - run test classes in [[b:parallel]] once contexts are shared and state is per-test; JUnit 5 parallelism turns a shared container from a bottleneck into a multiplier. - keep the unit suite as a separate, always-run task and the container suite as a second stage. Fast feedback is the entire point of the pyramid (12-architecture-patterns.clean-layered-building-it-for-real.q6). - [[o:one banner per configuration]] is the target. Everything else is cache misses you are paying for on every commit. :::

items.q: Two teams, two services, one broken deploy. How do contract tests catch it when neither side runs the other in CI?
items.a:
Spinning up the other team's service in your pipeline does not scale: you inherit their database, their fixtures and their outages. A contract test replaces the service with an agreement about the messages that cross the boundary. 
Consumer test          Contract (pact / schema)          Provider verification
expects {id, total}  ───────────────────────────────▶  replayed against the real provider
**The two shapes you will meet:** - [[g:consumer-driven contracts]] for request/response APIs: the consumer's test generates the contract; the provider's CI replays every consumer's expectations against the real implementation and fails before merge - [[g:schema compatibility]] for events: the registry rejects a producer change that would break existing consumers — the same idea, enforced at publish time
ChangeCompatible?Why
Add an optional fieldyesold readers ignore it
Remove a field a consumer readsnothe reader loses data it depends on
Rename a fieldnoa removal and an addition in one deploy
Narrow a type or add a required fieldnoold writers produce invalid messages
Add an enum valuecarefulfine only if readers handle the unknown case
:::warn What a contract test does not prove It proves the shape and the semantics you agreed on, not that the provider is fast enough, authorised correctly, or correct in its business logic. Those need their own tests. ::: :::deep - the contract lives with the [[b:consumer's expectations]], which is what makes it useful: a provider learns which of the forty fields anyone actually reads, and can drop the rest safely. - rolling deploys mean both versions run at once, so every change must be compatible in both directions for at least one release — the same expand/contract discipline as a schema migration (25-microservice.08-operational-concerns.q1). - for events, keep the registry check in CI rather than at runtime. Discovering incompatibility when the producer is already publishing is discovering it too late. - [[r:versioning the whole API]] is the expensive escape hatch. Additive change plus a deprecation window handles the vast majority of cases without doubling the surface you support. - record the contract for external partners too — a webhook payload is an API you can never take back once someone has parsed it (26-testing-strategy.testing-what-usually-breaks.q3). :::

items.q: How do you test logic that depends on time — expiry, schedules, time zones — without sleeping or waiting for midnight?
items.a:
Every `Instant.now()` scattered through the code is a hidden, untestable dependency. Inject a `Clock` and time becomes an argument you control. 
// the clock is a bean; production gets systemUTC, tests get whatever they need
class SeatHolds {
    private final Clock clock;
    
    boolean isExpired(SeatHold h) { return h.expiresAt().isBefore(clock.instant()); }
}
//
// no sleeping: move the clock instead of waiting for it
var clock = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-03-29T00:59:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);
var later = Clock.offset(clock, Duration.ofMinutes(6));
assertThat(new SeatHolds(later).isExpired(hold)).isTrue();
**Three time bugs worth a dedicated test each:** - [[r:expiry across a DST boundary]] — pick a zone that shifts and assert the duration, not the wall-clock difference - [[r:a schedule expressed in local time]] running on a UTC server, especially the 00:30 job that runs twice or not at all - [[r:comparison against a token or lock lease]] issued on another machine, where a few seconds of clock skew flips the result For anything genuinely asynchronous, waiting is still needed — but poll for the condition instead of guessing a duration: 
// flaky: passes on a fast laptop, fails on a loaded CI runner
Thread.sleep(500);
assertThat(repo.findById(id)).isPresent();
//
// deterministic in intent: bounded wait, fast exit, clear failure message
await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
       .pollInterval(Duration.ofMillis(50))
       .untilAsserted(() -> assertThat(repo.findById(id)).isPresent());
:::tip The smell to grep for `Thread.sleep` in a test is either a race you have not understood or a wait you have not bounded. Both are future CI failures. ::: :::deep - store and compare in [[g:UTC]], convert only at the edges. A test that passes only when the developer's machine is in one zone is a bug report about the code, not about the test. - `Clock.tick` is useful when the code assumes monotonically increasing timestamps: a fixed clock can make two events share an instant and hide an ordering bug. - for durations use a [[b:monotonic source]] (`System.nanoTime`) and never wall-clock subtraction, which can go backwards on an NTP correction. - schedules deserve a test that runs the cron expression through the same parser production uses; "every 5 minutes" and "at second 0 of every 5th minute" differ on the day the job takes six minutes (26-testing-strategy.testing-what-usually-breaks.q2). - when the assertion is about something that must *not* happen, a bounded wait is the only honest tool — assert the absence after the window, and keep the window short. :::

items.q: How do you write a test that actually reproduces a race, and why does a green concurrency test prove so little?
Your retry, timeout, circuit breaker and compensation logic has never run in a test. How do you inject failure on purpose?
items.a:
Resilience code is the least-executed code in the repository and the code you most depend on during an incident. It needs a seam where failure can be dialled in.
Failure to injectToolWhat it must prove
HTTP 500 / 429WireMock stubthe error is translated, not leaked to the caller
Slow responsefixed delay above the read timeoutthe client gives up in time and the thread is released
Connection reset / packet lossToxiproxy in front of the containerretry only fires on transient, idempotent calls
Repeated failurea stub that fails N timesthe breaker opens, then half-opens and recovers
Broker or DB downpause or stop the containerbackpressure and DLQ, not silent data loss
// the timeout is the contract: prove the client honours it before the pool drains
stubFor(post("/charges").willReturn(aResponse().withFixedDelay(5000)));
//
assertThatThrownBy(() -> payments.charge(cmd))
        .isInstanceOf(GatewayTimeout.class);
assertThat(hikari.getHikariPoolMXBean().getActiveConnections()).isZero();
verify(exactly(1), postRequestedFor(urlEqualTo("/charges")));   // no blind retry on a charge
**The three assertions people forget:** - the [[g:resource is released]] — pool connections, threads, the HTTP connection itself - the [[g:retry did not duplicate a side effect]] — a charge attempted twice must carry the same idempotency key (25-microservice.09-idempotency-the-central-link.q1) - the [[g:compensation actually ran]] and left the aggregate in a state the business accepts :::tip The order to write them in Happy path, then timeout, then duplicate delivery, then compensation. The last two are where money is lost, and they are the two nobody writes. ::: :::deep - test the breaker's [[b:state machine]], not its configuration: N failures open it, calls fail fast while open, one probe succeeds after the wait, traffic resumes (25-microservice.01-cascading-failure-retry-storm.q3). - a compensation test must include the ugly case — compensation itself failing. What the system does then is a business decision that belongs in a test, not in a runbook nobody reads (09-distributed-tx-fintech.distributed-transaction-patterns.q2). - [[r:retry on a non-idempotent POST]] is the classic double-charge. The test that catches it counts requests reaching the stub, not just the final status code. - chaos experiments in staging are the next step up, but they replace neither of these: an automated test fails a pull request, a chaos experiment fails a Wednesday afternoon. - keep the fake gateway scriptable — succeed, time out, return a duplicate, return a late success — so the same harness covers webhook and callback paths too. :::

items.q: A load test reports p99 = 80 ms while users complain. What is the test lying about?
items.a:
Most load tests measure a system that is politely waiting for them. Three things usually explain the gap between a green report and an angry user. **1. A closed model hides the queue.** A closed-loop tool with 50 virtual users sends the next request only after the previous one returns. The service slows down, the tool slows down with it, and arrival rate drops exactly when you needed it held constant. Real users do not behave that way. Use an [[g:open model]] with a fixed arrival rate and watch the queue grow. **2. Coordinated omission.** If a request stalls for 3 seconds, the requests that *would* have been sent during that window are never sent, and never counted. The worst latencies are simply missing from the histogram. Tools that keep a fixed schedule (`constant-arrival-rate`, corrected recording) close that hole. **3. Everything else is warm and empty.** A JIT that has not compiled, a cache that starts empty and a database holding 1,000 rows instead of 50 million benchmark a system you do not operate (04-rest-grpc-webflux.protocols.q1).
TestQuestion it answersRun it when
Loaddoes the target rate hold at the target latency?before every capacity change
Stresswhere does it break, and how?to find the real bottleneck
Spikedoes it survive a sudden 10x?flash sale, campaign, retry storm
Soakdoes it leak or degrade over hours?before a long weekend release
:::warn Averages are marketing Report p95, p99 and the error rate together with the achieved throughput. A p99 that looks good because half the requests failed fast is the most common false green. ::: :::deep - always record [[b:achieved rate vs target rate]]. If the tool wanted 500 rps and delivered 300, latency numbers describe a system serving 300 — the test found saturation and then measured the wrong thing. - watch the resource that saturates first, not the one you suspect: DB pool waiting time, thread pool queue depth, GC pause, Kafka lag (25-microservice.02-pool-exhaustion-connection-thread.q1). - warm up before measuring and keep the JIT profile realistic — a benchmark that never triggers C2 compilation reports startup performance forever. - a load test with [[o:one hot key]] and a load test with a realistic key distribution answer different questions; production usually has the hot key (25-microservice.06-hot-partition-db-bottleneck.q1). - end every run with an answer to "what is the bottleneck now?". A number without that sentence changes nothing. :::

items.q: A test fails once a week and passes on rerun. What is the policy, and why is high coverage no defence?
items.a:
A flaky test is worse than a missing one: it trains the team to rerun the pipeline instead of reading it, and the first real regression gets rerun away with it. **Where flakiness comes from, in the order you should check:** - time and waiting: `Thread.sleep`, a real clock, a timeout tuned to a fast laptop - shared state: a database row, a static field, a container reused without cleanup, test ordering - concurrency in the test itself, or an assertion racing an async handler - the environment: a fixed port, DNS, an external endpoint, an image tag that moved
SignalReality
90% line coveragelines executed; nothing about assertions
Branch coveragecloser, still blind to missing assertions
Mutation scoremutants introduced in the code that tests failed to kill
Escaped defectsthe only metric the business feels
A suite can execute every line while asserting nothing: [[r:coverage measures reach, not verification]]. Mutation testing flips the question. Change `>=` to `>`, delete a line, and see whether any test notices. High coverage with a low mutation score is the signature of tests that run the code and check nothing. :::tip A policy that works Quarantine on the second failure: the test moves out of the blocking suite the same day, with an owner and a deadline. Nothing gets muted quietly, and the main pipeline stays trustworthy. ::: :::deep - track flakiness as data — rerun history per test, sorted by failure rate. Without the list, everyone remembers a different culprit. - [[g:reproduce with the same seed, order and parallelism]]. Randomised execution order is worth enabling exactly because it surfaces hidden coupling early. - do not add a retry annotation to the whole suite. Retrying at the framework level converts a design problem into permanent noise. - run mutation testing on the [[b:domain package only]], where it is cheap and the results are actionable; running it over the whole codebase is where teams try it once and give up. - CI hygiene closes the loop: fixed test ordering off, parallelism on, containers pinned, one artifact promoted through environments, and every production bug arriving with the test that reproduces it (26-testing-strategy.what-a-test-is-for.q3). :::
